w: Lee Harvey Oswald was arrested here on November 22, 1963, minutes after Dallas officer J.D. Tippit was shot nearby -- the same afternoon Oswald was accused of killing President Kennedy. The Oak Cliff movie house still runs repertory screenings and events, forever tied to that one afternoon.

w: I.M. Pei designed the hall, Russell Johnson's Artec Consultants tuned its acoustics, and it opened in September 1989 after a decade-long campaign by the Dallas Symphony Association. Ross Perot's $10 million gift bought the naming rights, honoring Morton Meyerson, the campaign's leader.

w: This National Shrine Cathedral of Our Lady of Guadalupe dates from the late 19th century and seats the Catholic Diocese of Dallas. Its parish carries the second-largest Catholic membership in the US, drawing average Sunday attendance of 11,200 -- rare devotion for a downtown structure this old.

w: Opened in 2003 on a 2.4-acre site beside the Dallas Museum of Art, the Nasher houses Patsy and Raymond Nasher's collection of modern and contemporary sculpture -- one of the finest such holdings ever assembled by a single private collector, now set within a purpose-built garden museum at the heart of the Arts District.

w: Nicknamed 'Prado on the Prairie,' this 66,000-square-foot museum on SMU's campus holds one of the largest collections of Spanish art outside Spain, with works spanning the 10th to 21st centuries. It operates as its own division of SMU's Meadows School of the Arts, open to the public.

w: Opened in 1925 as the Hilton Hotel -- one of Conrad Hilton's earliest properties -- this Main Street corner building now operates as the Hotel Indigo Dallas Downtown. It's a contributing structure in both the Harwood Street and Main Street historic districts, across from Main Street Garden Park.

w: Called the 'birthplace of Dallas,' this small city park became the site of President Kennedy's assassination on November 22, 1963. Named for newspaperman George Dealey, it was declared a National Historic Landmark on the 30th anniversary of the shooting, preserving the surrounding streets and buildings.

w: Occupying the sixth floor of the former Texas School Book Depository, this museum overlooks the exact corner of Elm and Houston Streets where Lee Harvey Oswald allegedly fired on Kennedy's motorcade. w: Santiago Calatrava's cable-stayed arch spans the Trinity River, part of a planned trio of Calatrava crossings for the Trinity River Project -- only this one and the Margaret McDermott Bridge were built, the third was cancelled. It parallels the Ronald Kirk Bridge, now used only by pedestrians.

w: A dam across White Rock Creek created this 1,254-acre reservoir in northeast Dallas; the creek widens into the lake before spilling through the spillway and running south to join the Trinity River. It's the largest body of water inside the city, ringed by the east Dallas community around it.

w: Built for Magnolia Petroleum in Beaux-Arts style, this 29-story tower was for years the tallest building in Texas, having overtaken the Adolphus Hotel down the block. Now an upscale hotel, it carries a dual distinction as a Dallas Landmark and a listing on the National Register of Historic Places.

w: This 277-acre complex east of downtown was built out for the 1936 Texas Centennial Exposition and has stood as a National Historic Landmark and Dallas Landmark ever since. w: Nine bronze mustangs, one-and-a-half times life size, gallop through a fountain-fed watercourse at Williams Square, water jets timed to look like splashes kicked up by their hooves. Robert Glen's sculpture was commissioned in 1976 and installed in 1984; an adjacent museum shows a film on how the whole thing was made.
